source_pdf: Emerging challenges in implementing universal health coverage in Asia..pdf
title: Emerging challenges in implementing universal health coverage in Asia.
context: As countries in Asia converge on the goal of universal health coverage (UHC), some common challenges are emerging. One is how to ensure coverage of the informal sector so as to make UHC truly universal; a second is how to design a benefit package that is responsive and appropriate to current health challenges, yet fiscally sustainable; and a third is how to ensure “supply-side readiness”, i.e. the availability and quality of services, which is a necessary condition for translating coverage into improvements in health outcomes.
question: What are the three common challenges emerging in Asia as countries move towards universal health coverage (UHC)?
answer: The three common challenges emerging in Asia as countries move towards UHC are ensuring coverage of the informal sector, designing a fiscally sustainable and appropriate benefit package, and ensuring supply-side readiness.

title: Emerging challenges in implementing universal health coverage in Asia.
context: In China, the setting of enrollment targets for local government officials helped to raise enrollment rates (Liang and Langenbrunner 2013), while in Korea a mix of enrollment mandates and effective tracking of income and property has increased the administrative pressure to enroll (Jeong 2010). In Indonesia, which aims to fully cover its 70 million unenrolled informal sector workers by 2019, the government has initiated pilots to identify what works best. However, early results suggest subsidies, education, information and convenience will likely not make a large difference to enrolment among rural informal workers, with only a limited take-up among the urban informal sector (J-PAL 2015).
question: What are some country-specific strategies and challenges observed in Asia regarding the enrollment of informal sector workers in health coverage schemes?
answer: In China, enrollment targets for local government officials helped raise rates, while Korea used enrollment mandates and income tracking to increase administrative pressure; however, in Indonesia, initial results suggest subsidies, education, information, and convenience may not significantly increase enrollment among rural informal workers, with only limited take-up in the urban informal sector.

source_pdf: Emerging challenges in implementing universal health coverage in Asia..pdf
title: Emerging challenges in implementing universal health coverage in Asia.
context: A much easier and quicker approach to achieve high levels of coverage among the informal sector is to link coverage with citizenship or national residence, and to enroll the whole (as opposed to only the poor) informal population using general government revenues. Thailand embarked on this path and saw coverage rates improve significantly and relatively quickly (Li, Yu, Butler et al. 2011; Tangcharoensathien et al. 2011; Limwattananon, Neelsen, O’Donnell et al. 2014). Many other countries, including China, Korea and Taiwan, also rely on general revenues to cover the informal sector (Annear, Comrie-Thompson and Dayal 2015). This approach can also be more equitable than social health insurance; the latter is often regressive because of maximum ceilings on contributions that are typically imposed even when contributions are set proportional to income (Kwon 2009).
question: What are the key advantages of linking health coverage for the informal sector to citizenship or national residence and using general government revenues?
answer: Linking health coverage for the informal sector to citizenship or national residence and using general government revenues is an easier and quicker approach to achieve high coverage, as seen in Thailand, and can also be more equitable than social health insurance due to the regressiveness of contribution ceilings in the latter.

source_pdf: Emerging challenges in implementing universal health coverage in Asia..pdf
title: Emerging challenges in implementing universal health coverage in Asia.
context: Without a clear, rational process for defining and updating the benefit package what happens in practice is that thousands of discrete, and unpredictable, “rationing decisions” take place between client and provider at the point of service (Wong and Bitran 1999). These decisions are unlikely to result in either an efficient or an equitable distribution of health services and resources. Moreover, many benefit packages are somewhat out of date, having originally been designed when infectious diseases accounted for the majority of the overall burden of disease (Cotlear, Nagpal, Smith et al., in press). Today, in selecting services to include in the benefit package, consideration needs to be given to the increased share of non-communicable diseases (NCDs) in the burden of disease (IHME and World Bank 2013), as well as rapidly ageing populations, advances in medical technology, hospital-centric health systems, and the demands of a growing middle class (Somanathan, Bredenkamp and Pambudi et al. 2015), all of which will not only increase the demand for new services, but also exert upward fiscal pressure.
question: What are the practical consequences of lacking a clear and rational process for defining and updating universal health coverage benefit packages, and why are many existing packages considered out of date?
answer: Without a clear, rational process for defining and updating benefit packages, thousands of unpredictable "rationing decisions" occur at the point of service, leading to inefficient or inequitable distribution of health services, and many packages are outdated because they were designed when infectious diseases dominated the burden, now requiring consideration for non-communicable diseases, aging populations, and medical technology advancements.

title: Governance of artificial intelligence and personal health information
context: Effective health data governance remains an elusive goal for myriad reasons, and with ever increasing digital stockpiles of digitized PHI, a growing challenge (Hripcsak, 2014; Rosenbaum, 2010). First, digitized health data are created in health IT (HIT) systems spread across a variety of collaborative and competing organizations, including hospitals, physician practices, nursing homes, third-party payers (insurers) including state and federal governments, pharmacies, testing laboratories, and increasingly, by IT vendors that provide HIT systems. This results in the lack of data standardization and interoperability that currently presents substantive barriers to PHI data sharing and data use, including use in advanced analytics and AI applications. Second, regulations intended to limit the disclosure of personally-identifiable health data (such as HIPAA in the USA or GDPR in the European Union) have limited the flow and increased costs to researchers to access PHI data for societally sanctioned purposes (Lane and Schur, 2010).
question: What are two existing challenges to effective health data governance, excluding those directly related to AI's novel characteristics?
answer: Two existing challenges to effective health data governance are the creation of digitized health data across diverse and competing Health IT (HIT) systems, leading to a lack of standardization and interoperability, and regulations like HIPAA and GDPR, which limit the flow and increase costs for researchers seeking to access PHI data for sanctioned purposes.

question: How does patient-generated health data (PGHD) from health monitoring devices challenge existing health data regulatory oversight?
answer: Patient-generated health data (PGHD) from health monitoring devices and applications are developing outside of clinical settings and traditional health data regulatory oversight. The first branch is probably the largest, as it comprises those studies that seek to identify to what degree a certain governance scenario or management strategy addresses a specific governance -related value, such as sustainability, social justice, or economic efficiency. While these studies deal with individual governance-related values, they may still be very complex, as individual values may be highly multi-dimensional.
question: What are the three main branches into which existing research on governance-related values and water governance can be divided, and what is a characteristic of the largest branch?
answer: Existing research on governance-related values and water governance can be divided into three branches: in-depth case studies on individual governance-related values, policy-oriented literature, and water ethics, with the first branch being the largest as it comprises studies identifying how a governance scenario addresses a specific governance-related value.

title: Habitus Clivé and the Emotional Imprint of Social Mobility
context: The habitus represents a key conceptual tool in Bourdieu’s social theory, representing both a ‘structured’ and ‘structuring’ force in explaining social action. Bourdieu argued that those located in neighbouring positions in social space are socialised with similar ‘conditions of existence’ (meaning stocks of capital and distance from material necessity) and these conditions act to form the ‘structure’ of their habitus. In turn, this structure goes on to generate ‘structuring’ dispositions that guide social practice (Bourdieu, 1990: 60).
question: How does Bourdieu's social theory define the concept of 'habitus' in relation to social action and conditions of existence?
answer: In Bourdieu's social theory, habitus is defined as a key conceptual tool that acts as both a 'structured' and 'structuring' force in explaining social action. It is formed by the 'conditions of existence'—which include stocks of capital and distance from material necessity—of individuals located in similar social positions, and this structure then generates 'structuring' dispositions that guide social practice.

context: During such moments of profound change, when there is a mismatch between one’s (primary) habitus and the habitus required in a new field, Bourdieu (1977) argued that a hysteresis effect takes hold: ‘As a result of the hysteresis effect…practices are always liable to incur negative sanctions when the environment with which they are objectively confronted is too distant from that in which they are objectively fitted’ (Bourdieu, 1977: 78). Thus while Cerin’s habitus desperately tried to respond to a profound change of educational field, such a response took time and in the lag that followed she had to battle what Bourdieu (1977; 83) terms the ‘negative sanctions’ of relatives.
question: According to Bourdieu, what is the 'hysteresis effect' and how does it manifest for individuals experiencing profound social change?
answer: Bourdieu argued that the 'hysteresis effect' takes hold during moments of profound change when there is a mismatch between an individual’s primary habitus and the habitus required in a new field. As a result, practices are liable to incur negative sanctions when the environment is too distant from what they are objectively fitted for, manifesting as individuals battling 'negative sanctions' from relatives or others during the lag period of adaptation.

context: However, the links alluded to between UHC and equity are not straightforward: overall, it is unclear whether a focus on equity is supposed to enable progress in UHC (equity as a means), whether UHC is supposed to increase equity (equity as an end), or whether these are two distinct aims. Similarly, it is unclear whether equity is a value or principle orienting actions, or whether it is an objective of such actions. Some of the documents try and clarify the links between UHC and equity: for instance, the publications from the health financing department of the WHO recurrently use a model stating that equity in the distribution of resources is a UHC intermediate objective, and equity in service use is a UHC goal [ 39, 45]; a joint report views UHC as “the response to ” inequities [ 36]; and the 2017 Global monitoring report makes a clear distinction between equity and UHC [ 43].
question: What unresolved ambiguities were noted regarding the relationship between universal health coverage (UHC) and equity in global policy documents?
answer: The global policy documents showed an unclear relationship between UHC and equity, specifically regarding whether equity serves as a means to UHC progress, whether UHC aims to increase equity (equity as an end), or if they are separate goals. It was also unclear whether equity acts as a guiding value or principle, or as an objective of actions.

context: Treatment in an intensive care unit (ICU) staffed by appropriately trained intensivist clinicians improves survival in critically ill patients. However, many patients lack access to this level of care, particularly in small hospitals and in rural areas. ICU telemedicine is an innovative critical care delivery approach specifically designed to address this problem. Using ICU telemedicine, trained intensivist clinicians in regional hubs can monitor and treat patients at remote hospitals in conjunction with the bedside care team, potentially improving the overall quality of critical care.
question: What problem does ICU telemedicine aim to solve, and how does it function to improve critical care?
answer: ICU telemedicine is designed to address the problem of many critically ill patients lacking access to intensivist-staffed critical care, especially in small and rural hospitals. It functions by allowing trained intensivist clinicians in regional hubs to monitor and treat patients at remote hospitals in conjunction with the bedside care team, with the aim of improving overall critical care quality.

This national study aimed to improve upon those by including contemporaneous controls and using 90-day mortality as an endpoint.
question: What were the identified limitations of previous ICU telemedicine studies that this national study aimed to address?
answer: Previous ICU telemedicine studies were limited by being mostly single-center before-after studies that lacked concurrent controls. They often failed to follow patients past hospital discharge and presented conflicting results regarding mortality reduction, showing substantial reductions in some studies and no benefit in others. This national study aimed to address these limitations by including contemporaneous controls and using 90-day mortality as an endpoint.

context: Grubb (2004) as well as Bürer and Wüstenhagen (2009) stress that public grants as well as basic and applied R&D are required during the early phase of the innovation chain, while market-pull policies are necessary during later phases to reach full commercialisation (Figure 4.1). Additionally, optimal regulation may entail both a carbon price and an R&D subsidy to encourage innovation, and public R&D support is effective only if environmental policy (market-pull) is in place.

Results from a number of studies demonstrating no “dose–effect” relationship (i.e., no link between amount of treatment received—usually measured as number of sessions attended—and outcome variability) reinforce skepticism about attributing observed symptom change to treatment (Andrade et al. 2000; Garland et al. Lambert and Bickman (2004) proposed that observed decreases in symptom severity and/ or improvements in functioning after service entry should not necessarily be attributed to service effectiveness because such changes likely reflect predictable variation, including expected “regression to the mean.” Longitudinal modeling of expected variations in symptom severity and the assumption that children generally enter care when symptoms are most severe support this point.

answer: Reasons include the uncontrolled nature of studies, the lack of a “dose–effect” relationship between treatment amount and outcome variability, and the proposal that observed decreases in symptom severity may reflect predictable variation such as “regression to the mean.”

Thus, one can ﬁnd ﬁrms with the same level of productivity in either the formal or informal sectors over a considerable range in the productivity support, which is also inconsistent with the dual view of informality.
question: How does recent economic literature challenge the traditional dualistic view that formal and informal firms operate in entirely separate economic spheres?
answer: Recent economic literature challenges the dualistic view by showing that formal and informal firms coexist even within narrowly defined industries, contradicting the notion that they operate in separate economic spaces using different technologies. Additionally, studies reveal a substantial overlap in the productivity distributions of formal and informal firms within industries, indicating that firms with similar productivity levels can be found in both sectors, which is inconsistent with the dual view of informality.

context: This paper outlines a conceptual and methodological framework for investigating the politics of social protection, with a particular focus on explaining the variation in progress made by African countries in adopting and implementing social protection programmes. We propose that an adapted ‘political settlements’ framework that incorporates in sights from the literatures on the politics of welfare state development and discursive institutionalism can help frame elite commitment to social protection as an outcome of the interaction of domestic political economy and transnational ideas. This approach has the advantage of situating social protection within a broader policy context, as well as highlighting the influence of underlying power relations in society. Finally, the paper suggests a research methodology that can be employed to operationalise this approach, with a particular focus on process tracing and comparative case study research.

As such, the political settlement ‘refers to the balance or distribution of power between contending social groups and social classes, on which any state is based’ (Di John and Putzel 2009, p. 4). From this reading, institutions constitute not only the ‘rules of the game’ that influence individual behaviour, but also mechanisms for distributing rents within society (Khan 2010, p. 19, Di John and Putzel 2009). context: Khan (2010, p. 24) argues that structural transformation– namely, a shift in the economic basis of production and exchange from largely informal to largely formalised modes– is necessary to generate a sufficient tax base to distribute the resources needed to support the political settlement through the formal budgetary process. In the absence of such structural transformation, political elites will need to generate and distribute sufficient off-budget rents to keep powerful actors and groups bought into the political settlement. The result is that in developing countries, informal institutions, notably clientelism, are likely to prevail in the political realm – leading Khan (2010) to characterise all developing countries’ political settlements as ‘clientelist’. As such, the political settlements approach highlights the importance of informal, as well as formal institutions, and extends our analytical focus beyond class-based political mobilisation and formal political organisations operating in democratic contexts.
question: Why does Khan (2010) characterize political settlements in developing countries as 'clientelist'?
answer: Khan (2010) characterizes political settlements in developing countries as 'clientelist' because, without structural transformation to generate a formal tax base, elites must rely on generating and distributing off-budget rents, leading to the prevalence of informal institutions like clientelism in the political realm.

context: Of course, political settlements are often unfavourable to the expansion and effective implementation of social protection. Wherever social protection programmes are at least partly financed through domestic taxation, elite commitment to social protection expansion will require transformation of the underlying political settlement and a change in the existing distribution of rents– transferring resources away from powerful factions in order to provide resources for social programmes. In many cases, elites may be able to form a ruling coalition and establish the basic institutions required for political stability and economic growth without providing any form of social protection. In such circumstances, there will be few incentives for elites to agree to reduced rents through increased taxation and redistributive social spending, and the political settlement may constitute a barrier to expanding to social protection.
question: What factors within political settlements can impede the expansion and effective implementation of social protection?
answer: Political settlements can impede social protection expansion when elites can achieve stability and growth without it, thus having few incentives to agree to reduced rents through increased taxation and redistributive social spending, which is often required when programs are domestically financed.

context: There are three categories of scholarly consensus concerning the exaggeration of benefits linked to mega-events. The first suggests that the increase in direct spending attributable to the games may be a ‘gross’ as opposed to a ‘net’ measure, failing to account for the displacement of regular spending. Secondly, mega-events may crowd out regular business travellers in a particular region. question: What are the three categories of scholarly consensus regarding the exaggeration of benefits associated with mega-events?
answer: The three categories are: direct spending being a 'gross' rather than 'net' measure, the crowding out of regular business travelers, and a lower multiplier effect for mega-event spending compared to other local goods and services.

context: The point of departure for Ooms and Hammonds is a challenge set by Norman Daniels in his book Just Health [31]. After defending the ethical appropriateness of shared responsibilities for health at a national level, Daniels expresses pessimism at the possibility of extend-ing the ethical principles he used to a global level [30] and sets this as challenge for those interested in global health justice. In Taking up Daniels ’ Challenge, Ooms and Hammonds propose a mechanism for determining the amount of financial resources HICs should transfer to LMICs in order to realise the right to health. It should be noted that whereas Ooms and Hammonds ’ emphasis is on HIC obligations to ensure the fulfilment of the right to health in LMICs, our emphasis is on the obligations of LICs themselves in ensuring global health justice, particularly equity in global health financing.
question: What challenge did Norman Daniels pose in 'Just Health' that Ooms and Hammonds sought to address?
answer: Norman Daniels, in his book 'Just Health', expressed pessimism at the possibility of extending ethical principles of shared responsibilities for health from a national to a global level, setting this as a challenge for those interested in global health justice. Ooms and Hammonds addressed this by proposing a mechanism for determining the financial resources HICs should transfer to LMICs to realize the right to health.

context: The underlying moral reasoning here is that it is unjust to give assistance to coun-tries which are, or can be, above the targeted threshold of health-opportunities without assistance before suffi-cient assistance is given to others which have not yet reached, and cannot reach, the same threshold without extra assistance by virtue of their more constrained re-source capacities. In other words among LMICs there are some countries which are capable of fully financing the minimum health opportunities for their citizens without external assistance yet such countries are cur-rently receiving health aid before poorer ones get what they need. Our view is that when such countries claim external resources before worse-off countries get enough to cover their minimum health opportunities, then such claims (by better-off countries) are unjust. So far this category of moral reasoning is evidently lacking in the current manner in which global health is financed, par-ticularly international health resource transfers.
question: What moral argument do the authors present against providing external health assistance to better-off LMICs before poorer ones?
answer: The authors argue that it is unjust to provide assistance to countries that are, or can be, above the targeted threshold of health opportunities without external aid, before sufficient assistance is given to others that have not yet reached, and cannot reach, the same threshold due to more constrained resource capacities. They state that claims for external resources by better-off countries are unjust if worse-off countries have not yet received enough to cover their minimum health opportunities.

context: The push for making public services data available to the community started around mid- 2000s with the European Union directive encouraging greater realisation of the economic value of public data through its reuse in 2003. Conventionally, government departments retained public service data within their systems, with limited information being released to citizens and other stakeholders (i.e. businesses, charitable organizations, and NGO communities). However, the spread of digital governance and associated norms, such as responsiveness, accessibility and efficiency of public services, transparency and accountability (Carter and Weerakkody2008;W i l c o x2010;R a n ae ta l .2015), have motivated governments to exploit the potential of wider distribution and use of such data (Sivarajah et al.2015, 2016). The United States (US) is one of the first countries to mandate the use of open data in December 2009.
question: When did the initiative to make public services data available begin, and what key factors spurred governments to broaden its distribution?
answer: The initiative to make public services data available to the community began around mid-2000s with a European Union directive in 2003, which encouraged the realization of economic value through data reuse. Governments were motivated to exploit wider distribution and use of this data by the spread of digital governance and associated norms like responsiveness, accessibility, efficiency, transparency, and accountability. The United States (US) became one of the first countries to mandate the use of open data in December 2009.

context: Cross-sectional dependence is a phenomenon that is prevalent in most panel data regressions due to the interdependencies among countries especially those that are found within a particular region. Thus, to overcome the likelihood of biased estimates that characterise cross-sectional dependence in errors, this study opted for the Cross-sectionally Augmented ARDL (CS-ARDL) model based on the Pesaran’s (2006) Common Correlated Effect (CCE) approach for panel ARDL as rightly suggested by Chudik and Pesaran (2015). According to Pesaran (2006), cross-sectional means of both the dependent and regressors can be used to capture the unobserved common factors which can be inserted into the original model under the assumption of uncorrelated regressors and parameters. Also, the CS-ARDL assumes that the idiosyncratic error term is identically and independently distributed across country and time dimensions and that the cross-sectional average reverts to zero in root average square error as N, meaning that the linear combination of the cross-sectional averages of both dependent and explanatory variables can help account for the cross-sectional dependence in the errors (Ahmed, 2020).
question: What was the primary reason for selecting the Cross-sectionally Augmented ARDL (CS-ARDL) model as the estimation technique in this study?
answer: The primary reason for selecting the CS-ARDL model was to overcome the likelihood of biased estimates caused by cross-sectional dependence in errors, a prevalent phenomenon in panel data regressions due to interdependencies among countries. The model uses cross-sectional means of dependent and regressors to capture unobserved common factors.

This gap is considered a necessary corrective in psychology and the social sciences because injunctions to behave more sustainably have often relied on a depiction of a calculating, self-interested, and rational individual, which overlooks human fallibility.

context: The starting point for our analysis is that the rationality of the public sector is profoundly built on the interpretations, actions and ethical choices of actors involved in its practices. question: Describe the hot water treatment method for seed-borne diseases, including its advantages, potential drawbacks, and classic examples of its application.

question: What are the applications and limitations of dry hot air treatment and dry heat treatment (DHT) for seed disinfestation?
answer: Dry hot air treatment has been developed for controlling insects in grain stocks, applied in Australia at high capacities, but typically lacks good potential against fungal infections in seeds. Dry heat treatment (DHT), however, is an agrochemical-free method extensively used in countries like Korea and Japan to inactivate seed-borne viruses and other pathogens. For instance, it has been reported to reduce or eradicate anthracnose infection in lupine seeds when applied for 4-7 days at 65°C or up to 4 days at 70°C.

answer: Aerated heat treatment, also known as "aerated steam," involves a two-phase process: a heating phase with precisely controlled temperature and relative humidity, followed by a cooling phase to prevent seed injury. This method has shown potential for large-scale seed sanitization in a fluidized bed and has successfully controlled combined infections of S. nodorum and Fusarium spp. and T. caries on wheat, D. teres and B. sorokiniana on barley, and D. avenae and U. avenae on oat.

context: The problem is that current attempts at establishing standards for both financial and nonfinancial disclosure are still anchored to an idea of transparency based on a central entity that centrally seeks to “push” information out to the public—the central entity being the regulator that issues the standards or the firms that prepare and publish the accounts. The reality is that the public can currently pull that information from a varied and decentralized set of data sources. One effect is that its worth (from financial value to social and environmental values) is now more volatile than ever. Another effect is that a simple Tweet may make months of disclosure preparatory work collapse at the speed at which the news becomes viral, regardless of its facticity.
question: How do current attempts at setting disclosure standards fail to align with the modern reality of information access and communication?
answer: Current disclosure standard-setting attempts are still anchored to a "push" model of transparency from a central entity, while the public now "pulls" information from varied and decentralized data sources, making worth more volatile and allowing viral news, like a Tweet, to quickly undermine extensive disclosure work regardless of its facticity.

context: In the current politico-economic process, government agencies undertake some of their decisions based on cost benefit analyses (CBAs). CBAs are a corner stone of the welfare economic approach to public policy. However, the benefits from public goods are difficult to measure in monetary terms, as the marginal utility to consumers is not reflected in market exchanges. Inspired by well-being research, a promising method used to quantify the costs and benefits of public goods has been proposed, often called the “Life Satisfaction Approach” (see Frey, Luechinger, & Stutzer, 2010).
question: What limitation of traditional Cost Benefit Analyses (CBAs) for public goods has prompted the development of the "Life Satisfaction Approach"?
answer: The "Life Satisfaction Approach" was developed because traditional Cost Benefit Analyses (CBAs) find it difficult to measure the benefits of public goods in monetary terms, as the marginal utility to consumers is not reflected in market exchanges.

context: Taking reported subjective well-being as a proxy measure for individual welfare, it is possible to directly evaluate the utility provided by public goods. The marginal utility of public goods (or the disutility of public bads) is captured by correlating the amount of public goods (or public bads) by means of individuals’ reported subjective well-being, controlling for many other determinants on happiness. By comparing the marginal utilities of public goods to the marginal utility of income, the trade-off between income and public goods can be calculated. For example, the Life Satisfaction Approach has been used to value air pollution (Welsch, 2006; Luechinger, 2009; Levinson, 2012), flood hazards (Luechinger & Raschky, 2009), terrorism (Frey, Luechinger, & Stutzer, 2009), or wind turbines (Krekel & Zerrahn, 2017).
question: Explain how the Life Satisfaction Approach quantifies the utility of public goods and provide examples of what it has been used to value.
answer: The Life Satisfaction Approach quantifies the utility of public goods by using reported subjective well-being as a proxy for individual welfare, capturing marginal utility by correlating public goods or bads with individuals’ reported subjective well-being, and then calculating the trade-off between income and public goods by comparing their marginal utilities. It has been used to value air pollution, flood hazards, terrorism, and wind turbines.

context: This paper investigates the relationship between EU agricultural subsidies and agricultural labour productivity growth by estimating a conditional convergence growth model. We find that, on average, CAP subsidies increase agricultural labour productivity growth, but this aggregate effect hides important heterogeneity of effects of different types of subsidies. The positive effect on productivity comes from decoupled subsidies, i.e. Pillar I decoupled payments and some Pillar II payments. Coupled Pillar I subsidies have the opposite effect: they slow down productivity growth.
question: What is the main overall conclusion regarding the impact of EU Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) subsidies on agricultural labour productivity growth?
answer: On average, CAP subsidies increase agricultural labour productivity growth in the EU. However, this aggregate effect conceals important heterogeneity, with decoupled subsidies (Pillar I decoupled payments and some Pillar II payments) positively affecting productivity, while coupled Pillar I subsidies slow down productivity growth.

context: Our paper contributes to this literature by analysing the impact of the more than 50 billion euros annual subsidies of the EU’s Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) on agricultural productivity. In comparison with previous studies, we (a) use more accurate and complete CAP subsidy data, (b) disaggregate subsidy payments into payments of specific subsidy instruments, (c) have a wider coverage of EU regions, including the new member states (NMS), and (d) cover a longer and more recent time period than has been used before. Specifically, we use the Clearance Audit Trail System (CATS) dataset which includes all farm subsidies and details on the types of payments for all subsidy categories. Our analysis uses a regional conditional convergence model and covers the 2004-2014 period and 213 regions of the EU.
question: What key advancements in data and methodology did this study introduce compared to earlier research on the impact of CAP subsidies?
answer: This study advanced previous research by using more accurate and complete CAP subsidy data, disaggregating payments into specific subsidy instruments, expanding coverage to include a wider range of EU regions (including New Member States), and analyzing a longer and more recent time period (2004-2014) through a regional conditional convergence model with the CATS dataset.

question: Why are standard OLS or fixed effects estimators considered inappropriate for the dynamic panel model employed in this study?
answer: Standard OLS or fixed effects (FE) estimators are deemed unsuitable for this study's dynamic panel model because the lagged dependent variable is correlated with the model’s error term, leading to biased regression coefficients. Specifically, OLS estimators tend to be biased upwards, while fixed effects estimators are biased downwards in AR(1) panel models.

In principle, we can compute agricultural VA net of the effect of coupled payments by subtracting this CAP subsidy component from the agricultural VA. However, this approach implicitly assumes that the transfer efficiency of CAP payments is 100 percent, while studies have shown that the transfer efficiency is often lower, due for example to capitalization of CAP payments in land rents. Thus, following Olper et al. (2014) we measure agricultural labour productivity growth net of the effect of coupled CAP subsidies by first regressing the agricultural productivity growth (the dependent variable) on the coupled CAP subsidy component, and then keeping the residuals from that regression.
question: How did the study adjust the measurement of agricultural labour productivity growth to account for coupled CAP subsidy payments?
answer: To measure agricultural labour productivity growth net of coupled CAP subsidy payments and avoid endogeneity bias, the study first regressed the agricultural productivity growth (as the dependent variable) on the coupled CAP subsidy component, and then retained the residuals from this regression. This approach addresses the inclusion of coupled payments in agricultural VA and the often less than 100% transfer efficiency of CAP payments.

answer: Due to the difficulties in optimizing ecological, social, and economic aspects of sustainable development for present and future generations, concepts that embody dualities have arisen, including green economy/growth, green society, inclusive growth, and inclusive development.

If this hypothesis holds, capital deepening, driven by a fall in the price of capital, will increase the demand for skilled relative to unskilled labour.

question: What is the Integrated Macroeconomic Model for Poverty Analysis (IMMPA), and what are its key structural features for analyzing poverty?
answer: IMMPA is an applied macroeconomic model developed by Agénor and co-authors, characterized by a disaggregated production structure to study rural and urban poverty separately, and it captures the interdependent nature of production, demand, trade, and financial factors in a general equilibrium setting. A first important feature is its detailed treatment of the labor market.

title: Undoing Equivalence Rethinking Carbon Accounting for Just Carbon Removal
context: A just framing of carbon removal would require separate accounting and policy agendas on biotic and fossil fuel emissions. Such separation was already recommended several decades ago (WGBU, 1998) and has recently reappeared in the academic and political debate (NewClimate Institute, 2020; Skelton et al., 2020; Smith, 2021). Separation would help avoid the substitution of fossil fuel emission reductions for land-based actions that risk exacerbating climate injustices through environmental and social impacts. Rather than using biotic carbon removals to compensate for past, ongoing, or residual fossil emissions, restricting removals on a sectoral basis (e.g., land-based removals for land-based emissions) would encourage improved agricultural practices, minimize reliance on land sequestration, and force a faster transformation of sectors reliant on fossil fuels (Upton, 2019).
question: What does a just framing of carbon removal demand regarding biotic and fossil fuel emissions?
answer: A just framing of carbon removal demands separate accounting and policy agendas for biotic and fossil fuel emissions, which would help avoid substituting fossil fuel emission reductions for land-based actions and restrict removals on a sectoral basis to encourage improved agricultural practices and faster transformation of fossil fuel-reliant sectors.

context: We currently see rapid growth in the use of oﬀsetting to oﬀer “climate neutral” products and services and/or to make good on corporate and country-level net-zero pledges (Gross, 2020; NewClimate Institute, 2020). Many of these promises build on geographical equivalence, where oﬀsetting occurs through carbon removal—often in the form of aﬀorestation projects—in countries in the global South. This incentivizes delay—by providing cheap alternatives to diﬃcult or inconvenient emission reductions—and deepens climate injustice in several ways. question: How does the current growth in offsetting, based on geographical equivalence, contribute to climate injustice?
answer: The current growth in offsetting, often through afforestation projects in the Global South based on geographical equivalence, incentivizes delay in difficult emission reductions and deepens climate injustice by depriving poor nations of "cheap" carbon removal options, making their path to net-zero harder, while easing the path for wealthy nations.

context: Proposals for large-scale removal derive from modeled pathways that seek to stay within 1.5 or 2 ◦C warming limits. In the majority of these pathways carbon removal compensates for a temporary overshoot of the temperature target [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), 2014b, 2018 ]. This use of temperature overshoot and subsequent decline suggests that it does not matter when, over the next 80 years, mitigation actions occur, as long as the end-result by 2100 stays within agreed-upon temperature targets. It assumes substitutability between emission reductions in the near-term and further-oﬀ removals, a notion that is rapidly being institutionalized in net-zero targets.
question: What is the underlying assumption and core problem of temporal equivalence in climate policy related to temperature targets?
answer: The underlying assumption of temporal equivalence, institutionalized in net-zero targets, is that it does not matter when mitigation actions occur over the next 80 years as long as the end-result by 2100 stays within temperature targets, assuming substitutability between near-term emission reductions and further-off removals, often compensating for a temporary temperature overshoot.

context: For one, as Anderson and Peters (2016) point out, it neglects the diﬀerent risk proﬁles that characterize diﬀerent time horizons: we know what can be done in the present and what technologies are available, and can therefore reasonably assess their risks, ﬂaws, and economic and political feasibility. Future removals on the other hand often rely on technologies that are hypothetical at scale and their roll-out is therefore inherently more diﬃcult to assess. Second, signiﬁcant uncertainties remain concerning future climate feedback processes and tipping points (Tokarska and Zickfeld, 2015; Lenton et al., 2019; Creutzig et al., 2021), which could aﬀect the eﬀectiveness of carbon removal to reduce temperatures (Rogelj et al., 2018 , p. 127).

answer: Present mitigation actions have assessable risks, flaws, and feasibility because current technologies are known, while future removals rely on technologies that are hypothetical at scale, making their roll-out inherently more difficult to assess, and are subject to significant uncertainties concerning future climate feedback processes and tipping points.

context: Cutting across these diﬀerent concerns are the uneven intergenerational eﬀects of temporal equivalence. As Shue (2017) notes, the conﬂation of present with future climate actions entails a risk-transfer to future generations, in which the people deciding that future removal is a reasonable strategy to pursue are diﬀerent from those that will need to deal with any of the consequences arising should that strategy fail. Substituting near-term mitigation for future removals “sentences young people to either a massive, implausible cleanup or growing deleterious climate impacts or both’ (Hansen et al., 2016, p. 578). This occurs against a background where any costs of mitigating climate change in the face of insuﬃcient removal will be signiﬁcantly larger than today, and where those costs and consequences are likely to disproportionately fall on the poorest.
question: What are the uneven intergenerational effects resulting from temporal equivalence?
answer: Temporal equivalence results in uneven intergenerational effects by conflating present and future climate actions, which transfers risks to future generations who will face the consequences if future removal strategies fail, including potentially larger mitigation costs and deleterious climate impacts that disproportionately affect the poorest.

There are widespread oral health inequalities in outcomes and access, with the burden disproportionately affecting poorer, less educated members of society. Oral diseases are also the fourth most expensive disease to treat.

question: How do various countries fund and provide universal oral health care services?
answer: Countries like Austria, Denmark, Germany, Poland, Spain, Sweden, and Mexico provide basic dental care services through state-sponsored health insurance schemes funded by general taxation. Other countries, such as Greece, Turkey, and Finland, offer basic dental care through a mix of subsidized private practitioners and state-funded health services.

context: Additional sources of scale dependence arise from differences in the policy instruments that environmental and resource regimes use to manage human/environment relations and variations in the broader social settings within which individual regimes operate. What is more, differences in the broader socioeconomic and political settings in which specific regimes operate can prove highly important. context: In the context of the UK, power and control has been an ongoing contestation in central and local government relations over service determination, performance management and funding arrangements (Rhodes 1999; Wilson and Game 2011). There has been a gradual centralisation of funding that has not abated since the poll tax (a local tax on housing) was axed in the early 1990’s, and England has become the country with the most central control over local government funds of the major Western European Countries ( Ferry, Eckersley and van Dooren 2015). Since the early 1980s successive UK governments have also supplemented financial controls, through audit for financial conformance, with a range of centralised performance management frameworks that set out how local government should operate and what they should focus on (Seal 1999, 2003; Seal and Ball 2005, 2006, 2011). The performance of individual local authorities was then monitored against these frameworks through a comprehensive system of indicators and external audit and inspection, in order to try and create a “golden thread” that linked ministerial objectives and pronouncements with the administration of policy at the local level (Micheli and Neely 2010).
question: How has central control over local government funds evolved in England since the early 1990s, and what has supplemented financial controls in this period?
answer: There has been a gradual centralisation of funding in England that has not abated since the poll tax was axed in the early 1990s, making England the country with the most central control over local government funds of the major Western European Countries; since the early 1980s, UK governments have also supplemented financial controls through audit for financial conformance with a range of centralised performance management frameworks.

title: What should the African health workforce know about disasters Proposed competencies for strengthening public health disaster risk management education in Africa
context: We conducted a pilot research to develop and test a public health disaster risk management curriculum for training the African health workforce on DRM. We used mixed methods approaches including literature review to better understand the public health disaster risk management training needs and the associated knowledge and skills required by the African health workforce; qualitative research methodology to develop the core competencies and curriculum; knowledge translation and quantitative research methodology to test the applicability and feasibility of the competencies and curriculum. We implemented the curriculum development from 2009 to 2013, using a multistage consultative and qualitative process. A team of African emergency public health academicians and practitioners was assembled to: 1) conduct an in-depth review of existing emergency public health training programmes in the African Region; 2) identify knowledge, skills sets, and core competencies required by African HCWs to effectively engage in DRM; 3) develop a generic training curriculum for health DRM that is suited to the region; and 4) agree on the modalities for pilot testing the courses.
question: What methodology and process were employed for developing and testing the public health disaster risk management curriculum for the African health workforce?
answer: A pilot research using mixed methods approaches, including literature review, qualitative research, knowledge translation, and quantitative research, was conducted from 2009 to 2013. This involved a multistage consultative and qualitative process where a team of African academicians and practitioners reviewed existing programs, identified competencies, developed a generic curriculum, and agreed on pilot testing modalities.

question: What specific guidance did the US Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) issue in March 2013 regarding virtual currencies, and what were its implications under the Bank Secrecy Act (BSA)?

context: During the ‘Golden Age of welfare state expansion’ (1945-1975), although remaining in place in most countries, anti-poverty benefits lost most of their functional relevance in a context characterized by economic growth and Keynesian macroeconomic policies that aimed to guarantee full employment. At the same time, the origins of minimum income schemes date back precisely to this period, when last-resort income support schemes dropped the discretionary and ad hoc nature that had characterized them until then to resemble more and more fully fledged enforceable social rights (Ferrera, 2005). Despite different institutional designs, those schemes shared the vocation to serve as a residual layer of social support underneath universal and/or insurance-based social protection arrangements, providing for the “exceptional cases” with unusual needs that in a full-employment economy fell through the net of more comprehensive programmes and remained poor (Clegg, 2013; Nelson, 2003).
question: What was the functional relevance of anti-poverty benefits during the 'Golden Age of welfare state expansion' (1945-1975), and how did minimum income schemes evolve during this period?
answer: During the 'Golden Age of welfare state expansion' (1945-1975), anti-poverty benefits lost most of their functional relevance due to economic growth and full employment policies. Minimum income schemes originated in this period, evolving from discretionary last-resort support to enforceable social rights, serving as a residual layer for "exceptional cases" that fell outside more comprehensive social protection programs.
